text: Two hours and we only saw the ground floor, which was the right call. Wide aisles, benches, good light. The children were bored by hour two but not before. Lifts to the upper floors which is rare and I used one with my mother.
The main hall is excellent and flat. The upstairs galleries are a maze of narrow rooms with steps at every corner, and the lift help is enthusiastic but slow. Worth it for the hall alone.
The arms and armour hall is jammed with schoolchildren in the afternoon and you cannot move or hear anything. Came back at opening time on a Tuesday and it was completely different.
The sculpture garden is the reason to come and it is planted, level, and shaded. We were the only people in it for most of an hour and it cost nothing. Closed Mondays, which nobody tells you.
There is a step at the front door and a ramp to one side, which I did not know to ask about. The staff moved us through quickly and kindly. The garden is step free and we spent all our time there.
Two long rooms and the work is good but it is a small show and forty minutes is more than enough. Free is free, but do not plan an hour here.
The reading room is freezing, which in January is exactly right. Flat, a long table, and free to sit for as long as you like. I read for two hours and nobody said a word.

The painted ceiling kept my nine year old interested for the whole visit, which is a small miracle. No noise, no touching, and a lift if you need it. Closed for lunch, which is not written anywhere useful.
Turned up at one and the counter said it was closed for lunch until two, and we were not told that. Two hours wasted. The room is lovely, get the hours right first.

A lift to all three floors, toilets on every level, and a hearing loop at the desk. I have taken my mother to far worse and we were entirely comfortable. Husain, Raza, Sher-Gil, and the sculpture court at the top is the bit to end on.
Quiet, cool and small. An hour was enough for us and the top court is worth the lift. No cafe, so bring water, which I did not.
The ground floor is dim and you can walk straight past most of the good work without noticing. Ask for the map or start upstairs. Free and almost always empty, which is a shame.
Twenty minutes is exactly right and at night with the lights in the cast iron it is better than in daylight. It is a traffic island so stand on the far kerb, not the middle.
A traffic island with a child is a bad idea and we moved on after five minutes. The steps round the edge are a nice idea for sitting and a terrible one for anything else.
You are using it as a landmark, not visiting it. Fifteen minutes if you insist. It is genuinely useful for telling people where you are on the phone, which is the only real use.
Came out of the rain under the archway of the building next door with a coffee each and watched the clock for ten minutes. Not much of a visit, but a good pause.

Went to the Sunday service and were made to feel entirely welcome by the congregation, which was not something I expected. The iron roof is remarkable. The graveyard outside is the better half and it is flat.
Locked and you look through the grille, which is a disappointment on a weekday. The graveyard is worth it on its own and you can get in through a side gate, ask somebody.
A porter at the door, a cool tiled nave, and side chapels you can sit in quietly. Three steps at the entrance and then it is all level. Nobody minded me sitting there for half an hour.
Smaller and plainer than it looks in photographs, and the fittings that survived the Blitz are the interesting part, not the building. Still worth twenty-five minutes on a lane walk.

Still a working temple on a working lane, with a bell you ring yourself. Went at seven and the whole street was doing the same thing. Three steps into a small dark room, so I would not suggest a stroller.
I did not read the dress note properly and my husband was in a vest. We were turned away at the door and it was handled politely but that was the end of it. The temple is fine, we were the problem.

Non-Muslims are welcome in the courtyard and we spent a comfortable half hour there. The banding on the minaret is the thing to see. Shoes off means a bag of footwear, which nobody warns you about, and the side ramp is much easier than the front steps.

The courtyard is level and the toilets are actually good, which I did not expect. The main entrance is four steps and the ramp is round the side, so ask somebody straight away rather than struggling at the front.
We bought nothing and it was still the best hour of the Fort. The carvers work in the open and you can stand a metre away. Look up, the panels stacked at the kerb are ten feet high. Closed Sunday.
Fascinating and the lane is about four feet wide with a broken kerb on one side. We managed with a walking frame between us but it was tight and I would not recommend it if you are unsteady.
We could not get the pram through and the noise from the saws set our three year old off. It is a working street, not a family place, and I feel silly for bringing a toddler.
Three floors of second-hand everything and about ten degrees cooler than the street. The furniture floor is the real find. The staircases are steep and turn twice, so go up slowly.

I wanted the ground floor and it was fine for half an hour, but you cannot see the best of it without those stairs and I was not going to attempt them. Somebody should run a lift, because the value here is upstairs.
signalTags: stairs rule out the good floors

text: Squeezing a six year old through a labyrinth of narrow aisles and staircases with strangers shouting prices is not somewhere I would take a child. We left after twenty minutes and got chips.

Went at four in the afternoon and there were half a dozen people. Fruit stalls, a lift or a ramp to the gallery, toilets inside, and the pram went anywhere we wanted. Completely different from the reputation.
Went at one and it was a solid wall of people and shouting. Come at ten or after four. The mali puri upstairs is worth the lift if you can get to it.
Flat iron hall, level floor, public lift, clean toilets, and a bench on the gallery. My husband had no trouble at all and we ate lunch up there. This is the market to send an older person to.
Free, empty, and my son could hold a gold bar, which he will not stop talking about. Four small rooms, an hour is plenty, and there is a step at the door plus a lift upstairs.
I asked at the counter about the hearing loop and they had one, which I did not expect from a bank museum. Cold, quiet, and there is a bench in every room.
You need photo ID and a form and then they fetch the box, and we were told to come back in forty minutes. Nobody told us that on the way in. Not worth planning a short window around.

Empty, cool, and the ceiling is the reason. The caretaker spent ten minutes explaining the bimah without being asked. Level access through the side gate. It is a working synagogue so check it is not a Jewish holiday first.
Went on a Saturday and the gate was locked with no notice and no explanation. Somebody in the lane told me it was a holiday. Frustrating, and there is nothing on the door to tell you.

A Marathi play in a theatre from the 1890s, for a hundred and fifty rupees, with a lift to the circle. The audience was local families and they laughed at things I did not follow, which was the best thing.
Booked nothing and got there fifteen minutes late to find the door shut and the show half done. Now they will not take bookings over the phone, which is the real problem.

We spent three hours here and would happily have spent four. The marble foyer alone is worth the entry, the food court in the old lobby is good, and it is the most reliable wet-weather afternoon in the Fort with a twelve year old.
There is a hearing loop at the box office and staff who did not make a fuss about asking. Step-free from the street to the seat. The lift to the upper circle is slow but it exists.
I had ninety minutes free and looked at this on my phone and rejected it on duration alone, which was the right call. Two and a half hours plus a queue is not a ninety minute plan.
I walked in off the street with no plan, sat in the courtyard with a coffee, and read a newspaper for an hour. Nobody asked for enrolment, there is a lift, and the building is beautiful.
Attended a free talk in the auditorium and the hearing loop worked. Courtyard cafe does not need you to buy anything to sit, which is rare in this district.
Brought photo ID, booked the week before, and they had the box ready. Nineteenth century village surveys in a supervised room. A cage lift and a staircase, so plan for a step either way.
I did not book, walked in, and was told to come back tomorrow with the form filled in. Entirely my fault, and it cost me a morning.

We got plastic chairs at a table for five at half past nine, which is not guaranteed. The kebabs are the real thing and the mithai afterwards is the reason to stay. Get there before nine if you want a table.
The chairs are on the road edge and it is loud and hot and I did not enjoy it. My son did enormously. Come early, and do not come if sitting down properly matters.

Two hours setting type and pulling prints on a real Heidelberg. My hands were black for two days and I have printed a card for every birthday since. There is no short version of this and you need a day of it.
I love what they do and I could not get to the bench, which is up two steps and then a narrow aisle. The printer was kind about it and I watched from a chair, but I did not do the thing I booked for.

A stone cellar with six artists in it and a track light each. Thirteen steps down with a turn, donation at the door, and one of them spent ten minutes talking to me. Thursday, eight in the evening, nobody there but me.
Last Friday opening. Seventy people in a room for thirty and we could not get in. The work is good but I would go on a Tuesday, and thirteen steps is thirteen steps.
Watching real printers set type through a glass wall is a genuinely good way to spend forty-five minutes with a twelve year old. Flat, cool, and a printer who explained everything we asked.
Step-free and cool, which is what I need. The machines are enormous and I found it more industrial than interesting. Still worth forty-five minutes on a hot day.
Ninety minutes of treadling a pit loom and my stole is crooked and I love it. The noise is constant and there is no sitting out, but the rhythm of it is the best thing I have done in Mumbai.
Narrow stairs up to a first floor room and then an hour and a half standing at a loom. I knew about the stairs and forgot about the standing. My back was fine for two days.

The first hour of ghazal is extraordinary and the second hour of qawwali changes the room completely. No microphone anywhere, which you feel in your chest. Step-free at the door, and sitting on the floor is not adjustable.
Six of us and we were allocated cushions at the front, which nobody told us to ask for. Book a day ahead. Chai afterwards outside is part of it.
Wonderful music that I could not follow because I have no hearing loop and there is not even a microphone to lose. Sitting cross-legged on the floor for two hours also finished me. Not for us.

Two hundred and fifty rupees, a steel chai, and nobody cares that I have been on the same chair for two hours. Exactly what a working lunch should be. One step into the room and the pavement outside is wide enough for two chairs.

Cheap and cheerful and the step into the room was manageable, but there is one step and no toilet, and the chairs have no arms. I ate, I would come back, but I would not plan a comfortable hour here with my mother.
You stand on the pavement and look up at the tiles, and that is entirely the visit. Thirty-five minutes is generous. Good place to stop and work out where you are before the next thing.
Lovely facade and absolutely nothing to do, which I knew. Useful because it is on the way and the pavement is wide enough to stop on. There is a car repair next door, so it is not quiet.
